title: PCA as variance maximisation
promptMarkdown:
Let $\mathbf{X}$ be an $N \times D$ matrix of centred observations and $\boldsymbol\Sigma = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}/N$ its sample covariance (W1D4 Tutorial 2).

1. Show that for a unit vector $\mathbf{w}$ the sample variance of the projections $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}$ equals $\mathbf{w}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{w}$.
2. Prove that the unit vector maximising this variance is an eigenvector of $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ for its largest eigenvalue, and that the maximal variance equals that eigenvalue. State what you use about $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ (symmetry, positive semidefiniteness) and where.
3. Let $\mathbf{w}_i$, $\mathbf{w}_j$ be eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues. Prove that the score vectors $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}_i$ and $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}_j$ are uncorrelated. Explain briefly why the second component is therefore the top eigenvector of $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ restricted to the orthogonal complement of the first.
4. Compute the principal components and the fraction of variance explained by the first component for $\boldsymbol\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ (a synthetic covariance, not from data).
5. Explain what changes in the components if one variable is rescaled by a constant, and why centring is required for part 1 to be a variance.
hintLadder: The projections have mean zero because the columns of $\mathbf{X}$ do; their variance is $\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\|^2/N$.

Maximise $\mathbf{w}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{w}$ subject to $\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{w} = 1$ with a Lagrange multiplier, or expand $\mathbf{w}$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis (the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices) and bound the Rayleigh quotient.

$(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}_i)^\top(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}_j)/N = \mathbf{w}_i^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{w}_j = \lambda_j\mathbf{w}_i^\top\mathbf{w}_j$; symmetric matrices have orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues.
The characteristic polynomial of the $2 \times 2$ matrix is $(3 - \lambda)^2 - 1$.

deterministicChecks.description: the characterisation must be proved for general D, not checked in examples
a Lagrange multiplier, Rayleigh quotient or eigenbasis argument appears
the first component explains 4/6 = 2/3 ≈ 66.7% in the 2 × 2 example

criteria.criterion: Projections have zero mean (centred columns); variance ‖Xw‖²/N = wᵀXᵀXw/N = wᵀΣw.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Both the zero-mean point and the identity.

criteria.criterion: Lagrangian wᵀΣw − λ(wᵀw − 1) gives Σw = λw, so stationary points are eigenvectors with variance λ and the maximum is the largest eigenvalue; or the Rayleigh quotient bounded by λ_max via the spectral theorem (symmetry gives a real orthonormal eigenbasis; PSD gives λ ≥ 0).

levels.label: met
levels.description: Complete, with the properties of Σ named where used.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Stationarity shown, maximality or the spectral theorem not invoked.

criteria.criterion: Cov = w_iᵀΣw_j = λ_j w_iᵀw_j = 0 by orthogonality of eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix for distinct eigenvalues; hence the second component maximises variance within the orthogonal complement, where Σ's top eigenvector is the second eigenvector overall.
Eigenvalues 4 and 2; eigenvectors (1, 1)/√2 and (1, −1)/√2; PC1 explains 4/6 = 66.7%.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Eigenvalues right, vectors or share wrong.

criteria.criterion: Rescaling a variable by c multiplies its variance by c² and its covariances by c, changing eigenvectors and eigenvalues (PCA is not scale-invariant); without centring wᵀXᵀXw/N is a second moment, not a variance, and the first direction points towards the mean.

checkExamples.label: correct proof
checkExamples.text: For arbitrary D: the columns of X have mean zero, so Xw has mean zero and its sample variance is ‖Xw‖²/N = wᵀXᵀXw/N = wᵀΣw. Maximise wᵀΣw subject to wᵀw = 1 with a Lagrange multiplier: ∇(wᵀΣw − λ(wᵀw − 1)) = 2Σw − 2λw = 0, so Σw = λw and the variance at a stationary point is wᵀΣw = λ; Σ is symmetric, so by the spectral theorem it has a real orthonormal eigenbasis and the maximum over the unit sphere is the largest eigenvalue, attained at its eigenvector (Σ is PSD so all eigenvalues are nonnegative). For eigenvectors w_i, w_j with distinct eigenvalues, Cov(Xw_i, Xw_j) = w_iᵀΣw_j = λ_j w_iᵀw_j = 0 because eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal; restricting to the orthogonal complement of w_1, the same argument gives the second eigenvector. Example: (3 − λ)² − 1 = 0 gives λ = 4, 2 with eigenvectors (1,1)/√2 and (1,−1)/√2; PC1 explains 4/6 = 2/3 ≈ 66.7%. Rescaling a variable by c scales its variance by c² and covariances by c, so the components change; without centring the quadratic form is a second moment and the first direction points at the mean.

checkExamples.label: checked in low dimensions only
checkExamples.text: For n=1 and n=2 the direction of largest spread is the first component, so PCA maximises variance. The first component explains half the variance.
